contrasts.label: Beau or bout?
contrasts.description: Listen for the final rounded vowel. These pairs contrast close-mid /o/ with close /u/; neither category is the open-mid /ɔ/ of the separate o ouvert lesson.

l1Notes.note: Both vowels are taught as single French vowel categories. The English vowels in go and boot are approximate comparisons, not target recordings.
The letters ou represent /u/ in these examples; attend to the sound before enabling spelling hints.

contrasts.label: Chat or chant?
contrasts.description: Listen to the final vowel: oral /a/ or nasal /ɑ̃/. The nasal vowel is one sound, with no added n or ng consonant in these isolated words. Its oral quality may differ too.

l1Notes.note: Listen for a nasal vowel rather than a vowel followed by an English n or ng.
The final written n, ng, and nt do not add a spoken nasal consonant to these isolated target words.

pairs.note: Select the dictionary /ʁa/ variant. TLFi also documents /ʁɑ/: audio must be reviewed against the selected /a/ target.

contrasts.dialectNote: Northern reference Metropolitan French broad phonemic notation. TLFi gives rat /ʁa/ and also reports historical /ʁɑ/ variation; this candidate explicitly selects /a/. A recording with oral /ɑ/ must not be silently accepted for the /a/ category. Nasal quality varies across regions and speakers.

contrasts.label: Beau or bon?
contrasts.description: Listen to the final vowel: oral /o/ or nasal /ɔ̃/. In these isolated words, the nasal spelling does not add a separate n consonant. The contrast can include vowel-quality differences as well as nasalization.

l1Notes.note: Bon does not end with the n consonant of English bone. Listen to its complete vowel.
Compare whole vowel categories. Adding a spoken n to /o/ is not the target for bon, pont, or ton.

contrasts.dialectNote: Northern reference Metropolitan French, in isolation. Broad /ɔ̃/ does not require a literal nasalized copy of oral /o/ or /ɔ/ in every voice. Bon here is isolated masculine /bɔ̃/; its feminine and some liaison forms are different. Do not merge this lesson with oral /o–ɔ/.
